hints: Start by breaking the phrase into its two parts - what does infectious mean on its own, and what does disease mean on its own?
Now link both ideas to the story - what is the baculovirus doing to the insect, and how would it get from one feeding larva to another on sprayed plants?
walkthrough:
What Makes Something a Disease**
A disease is a loss of normal functioning that causes harm, ill health or death. Here the virus kills insect pests, so it clearly has a harmful effect on the insect body.

What Makes It Infectious**
Infectious means caused by a pathogen that can be transmitted between hosts. Baculovirus is the causative organism and polyhedrons sprayed on leaves are ingested by other larvae, so transfer from insect to insect occurs.
Final answer: Baculovirus is a pathogen that causes disease / harm / death in insects and is transmissible from one insect host to another, so the disease is infectious.

hints: Remember the polyhedron is made of protein. Think about what two general gut conditions normally act on proteins in food.
For each condition, think about the mechanism - how does pH affect bonds holding shape, and what do proteases do to the chain itself?
walkthrough:
Unfolding by Extreme pH**
The insect gut is highly alkaline. Excess H+ or OH- ions disrupt hydrogen bonds and ionic bonds between R groups, so the polyhedrin proteins lose their 3D shape and unfold. This is denaturation.

Cutting by Gut Enzymes**
The gut also contains digestive hydrolytic enzymes such as extracellular proteases. At their optimum pH they catalyse hydrolysis of peptide bonds between amino acids, breaking the polyhedrin chains into smaller peptides and releasing the virus.
Final answer: Highly alkaline pH disrupts hydrogen and ionic bonds, denaturing polyhedrin; proteases / hydrolytic enzymes hydrolyse peptide bonds at optimum pH, breaking down the polypeptides.

hints: Look at what each figure shows you - Fig. 3.1 is a list of amino acid names, Fig. 3.2 A is one folded chain with coils and arrows, Fig. 3.2 B is three chains together.
Recall the four levels of protein structure in order and match each figure part to a level.
For the folded single chain, think about local coiling versus overall 3D folding held by R-group bonds.
For the whole molecule, count how many polypeptides are interacting and state the level name clearly.
walkthrough:
Primary Structure From Fig. 3.1**
Fig. 3.1 shows the order of amino acids: met - pro - asp - tyr - ser - tyr - arg - pro - thr - ile and so on for 245 amino acids. Adjacent amino acids are joined by peptide bonds. That sequence is the primary structure.

Secondary Structure From Fig. 3.2 A**
In the ribbon diagram the coiled regions are alpha-helices and the flat arrows are beta-pleated sheets. These regular local foldings formed by hydrogen bonding between C=O and N-H groups of the backbone are the secondary structure.

Tertiary Structure From Fig. 3.2 A**
The whole single polypeptide is further folded and coiled into a precise 3D shape. That overall shape is held by interactions between R groups / side chains: hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions and disulfide bridges. That is the tertiary structure.

Quaternary Structure From Fig. 3.2 B**
Fig. 3.2 B shows three identical folded polypeptides associated together to make one polyhedrin molecule. The assembly of more than one polypeptide chain is the quaternary structure.

Final answer: Primary: sequence of 245 amino acids joined by peptide bonds, e.g. met-pro-asp-tyr-ser-tyr-arg-pro-thr-ile. Secondary: alpha-helices (coils) and beta-pleated sheets (flat arrows). Tertiary: folding/coiling of polypeptide held by R-group interactions - H-bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions, disulfide bridges. Quaternary: three identical polypeptides interacting as shown in Fig. 3.2 B.

hints: Think about the direction of information flow - DNA triplet to mRNA codon to amino acid - and whether that step is one-to-one.
Recall the numbers: how many different codons exist, and how many amino acids do they code for? What must that mean?
Focus on which position in the codon is most variable, and why that prevents working backwards from protein to exact DNA.
walkthrough:
Many Codons For One Amino Acid**
Protein synthesis uses triplets of bases read as mRNA codons. The code is degenerate, meaning most amino acids have two or more different codons. So seeing serine or proline in the chain does not tell you which codon was used.

Why Degeneracy Happens**
There are $64$ possible codons but only $20$ amino acids used in proteins. Often only the first two bases are the same and the third base can vary. That wobble in the third position creates the uncertainty.

You Cannot Work Backwards Exactly**
Because of this many-to-one relationship, plus stop codons that do not code for amino acids, the same 245 amino acid sequence could be produced by many different DNA nucleotide sequences. The amino acid order therefore cannot specify the gene sequence.

Final answer: The genetic code is degenerate: most amino acids are coded for by more than one codon, often differing in the third base. There are 64 codons for 20 amino acids, so the exact triplet / nucleotide sequence cannot be deduced from amino acids alone.
